newsitem.title: USA: Let markets rule on dollar, U.S. economists say.
newsitem.headline: Let markets rule on dollar, U.S. economists say.

text.p: U.S. economists on Wednesday praised Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin's hands-off approach to the rising dollar, and even those industry groups who stand to lose seemed resigned to continued dollar strength.
Rubin's approach was both laudable and inevitable since U.S. economic prospects were so much better than overseas partners like Germany and Japan, the economists said.

"It is really the superb performance of the U.S. economy against the rest of the world -- low inflation, low unemployment, the seventh year of expansion, very strong productivity -- that is making the dollar THE currency to hold," said Allen Sinai, chief global economist for Primark Decision Economics Inc in Boston.

"Market fundamentals are driving the dollar to record levels and they will take it to further highs," Sinai predicted. He said it was always preferable to let fundamentals "call the tune" in setting relative values of the dollar, the Japanese yen and the German mark.
The dollar touched a 4-1/2-year high of 127 yen on Wednesday and a three-year peak of 1.7270 marks before closing lower against both currencies in New York trading.

Even lawmakers from districts hit hardest by a higher dollar, like Michigan's car-making centers, doubted that there was any effective way to brake the dollar. Pushing partners like Japan to let more imports in was the favored approach.
"As difficult as it is to successfully press Japan on opening its markets, it's even more difficult to try to control currencies directly," said Democratic Rep. Sander Levin of Michigan.
Levin said he and other lawmakers intended to tell Rubin in a Thursday meeting that their favored policy remedy was a tougher approach to Japan.
"The more that direct intervention in currency markets is difficult, the more important it is that we press on these other fronts," Levin said.

But manufacturing industries may be getting set to campaign for currency intervention, fearing the dollar's rise will price them out of foreign markets and foster a rising tide of cheaper foreign-made goods.

Gordon Richards, an economist for the National Association of Manufacturers (NAM), said 60 percent of its members complained in a survey three weeks ago that their sales and profits were being hurt by the rising dollar.
Fully 50 percent said then that if it went higher -- as it has since done -- then the United States should actively intervene in currency markets.
Richards said NAM directors were meeting for three days starting on Thursday, with the dollar's value certain to be discussed.
"There is abundant evidence to suggest that, in the short term, intervention can be a powerful and credible policy tool," Richards said.

Rubin, just back from a major Asian trip that took him to Japan, the Philippines and Vietnam, has studiously avoided saying anything more than that a strong dollar restrains U.S. inflation and keeps interest rates low. The currency has been strong for "quite some time," he adds.

Economist Sung Won Sohn of Norwest Corp in Minneapolis, said he strongly believed the Treasury "should do nothing" to try to affect currencies directly unless values were "gyrating." There is no sign that imbalances are developing, he added.
"What we are seeing today and yesterday is not disorderly," Sohn said. "A lot of people have been saying the dollar is too strong but in the immediate future I think it'll continue to appreciate.
"The United States is now the number-one productive economy in the world," Sohn said, which attracts capital and investment and adds to the dollar's luster."
